newsitem.title: USA: Heating oil hits highest level in entories.
newsitem.headline: Heating oil hits highest level in entories.

text.p: Heating oil prices soared again Thursday on worries over low inventories in the United States and Europe as Western oil companies and consumers start preparing for the coming winter, but the market was unable to hold on to its gains.

Heating oil for October delivery gained more than 1 cent to 72.80 cents a gallon Thursday after rising 2.08 cents on Wednesday. The price was the highest since early November 1991 after the Gulf War. Heating oil later gave up those gains and was off 0.67 cent at 71.10 cents in late trading.

Heating oil has jumped more than 25 percent in the last three months on worries over tight supplies in the United States and Europe. The surge in prices has also helped boost prices of crude oil and gasoline.
October gasoline rose 0.05 cents to 63.15 cents a gallon. November crude oil fell 26 cents to $24.20 a barrel.
"I think people are expecting a hard winter, with strong demand and supplies low," one trader said of the latest rise in heating oil.
Markets for heating oil in New York and Rotterdam in the Netherlands both have seen premiums for prompt delivery rise quickly over the past couple of days.
Refiners and traders have bought heavily on futures markets to protect themselves against higher prices this winter. Speculators have bet on further price gains.
"It would be foolish to bet against this market going higher," said one dealer in London. "It would be like standing in front of a freight train."

Industry and government reports this week showed heating oil and diesel stocks were about 30 percent below 1995 levels in the Northeast, the nation's largest market for home heating oil. Stocks in Europe's biggest market, Germany, were also well below normal.
Industry analysts said the drive by oil companies to cut costs the last two years by delivering "just-in-time" would make markets vulnerable to further price spikes over the winter months.

In addition, the markets are doing without several hundred thousand barrels of oil a day from Iraq after a U.N.-backed oil-for-food deal was put on hold indefinitely after Baghdad's military incursion into Kurdish areas earlier this month.
In other markets, gold prices slumped after news the International Monetary Fund may sell 5 million ounces of gold from its reserves to help the world's poorest nations.
October gold fell $1.70 to $380.70 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.
Platinum prices tumbled in sympathy, with the metal falling to $385.25 an ounce in London, the lowest since Jan. 31, 1994.
